title: Integration begins with a derivative
lead: Look for the function whose rate of change you have been given.
ideas: If $F\prime(x)=f(x)$, then $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$. For instance, $x^3$, $x^3+4$ and $x^3-9$ all have derivative $3x^2$. An indefinite integral records this whole family: $$\int f(x)\,dx=F(x)+C.$$ The constant is determined only when an extra value is given.

An integral with limits is different: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is accumulated signed change. If a rate is below zero, its contribution is negative. A definite integral is a number; an indefinite integral is a family of functions.
Linearity is useful: $\int(af+bg)=a\int f+b\int g$. Integration does not distribute over products or quotients. Choose a method after simplifying the integrand.

examples.title: Recover a quantity
examples.question: $F'(x)=9x^2-4$ and $F(1)=8$. Find $F(x)$.
examples.plan: We know the derivative and one value of $F$. Integrate to get a family of functions. Then use $F(1)=8$ to choose the correct member.

steps.why: Integration is linear, so you integrate a sum term by term. The power rule raises the power by one and divides by the new power.
Every function in this family has derivative $9x^2-4$. The constant $C$ disappears when you differentiate.
The extra value selects exactly one member of the family.

steps.do: Check: $F'(x)=9x^2-4$ and $F(1)=3-4+9=8$. Both conditions are true.
steps.why: Differentiating the answer is the fastest check for any integral.

examples.title: Why the interval matters
examples.question: Find $\int \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx$.
examples.plan: The power rule fails for $x^{-1}$ because it divides by $n+1=0$. Look for a function whose derivative is $\dfrac1x$.

steps.do: Try the power rule: $\dfrac{x^{0}}{0}$ is not defined.
steps.why: So $\int x^{-1}\,dx$ needs a different rule.
This covers the positive side of zero.
The chain rule gives the same derivative on the negative side.
The modulus makes one formula work on both sides. The point $x=0$ is always excluded, so never integrate $\dfrac1x$ across zero.

trap: Do not write $\int_a^b f=F(b)+C$. The same constant cancels from $F(b)-F(a)$.

types.title: Find an antiderivative by inspection
types.question: Find an antiderivative of $\sin 2x$.
types.plan: Ask: which function has derivative $\sin 2x$? Guess, differentiate the guess, then fix the number in front.

steps.do: Guess $-\cos 2x$, because the derivative of $\cos$ gives $-\sin$.
steps.why: A minus sign in front of cosine makes the derivative a positive sine.
The chain rule brings out the factor $2$ from the inner $2x$. The result is twice the required function.
A constant factor passes through the derivative unchanged.

types.title: Expand a product first
types.question: Evaluate $\int (2x+1)(x-3)\,dx$.
types.plan: There is no product rule for integration. Multiply out the brackets, then integrate each power of $x$.

steps.why: Now the integrand is a sum of simple powers.
Use $\int x^n\,dx=\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$ for each term. The constant $-3$ integrates to $-3x$.

steps.do: Check: the derivative is $2x^2-5x-3$, which equals the expanded integrand.
steps.why: This confirms each coefficient.

types.title: Find a curve from its gradient
types.question: The gradient of a curve at any point $(x,y)$ is $2x+3$. The curve passes through $(1,\,2)$. Find its equation.
types.plan: Gradient means $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$. Integrate it to get $y$, then use the given point to find $C$.

steps.why: The gradient of a curve is the derivative of $y$.
This is a family of parallel curves, one for each value of $C$.
The point fixes which curve of the family we need.

title: Build a reliable formula bank
lead: Every standard integral is a differentiation rule read backwards.
ideas: Power rule: increase the power by one, then divide by the new power. $$\int x^n\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C,\qquad n\ne-1.$$ This rule cannot be used when $n=-1$, because the denominator would be zero.
Reciprocal rule: $$\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx=\ln|x|+C,\qquad x\ne0.$$ Use this on an interval that does not contain zero.
Exponential rule: $$\int e^{ax}\,dx=\frac{e^{ax}}{a}+C,\qquad a\ne0.$$ Differentiating $e^{ax}$ introduces a factor of $a$, so integration divides by $a$.
For a positive base other than one: $$\int b^x\,dx=\frac{b^x}{\ln b}+C,\qquad b>0,\ b\ne1.$$

Trigonometric rules: $$\begin{aligned}\int\sin x\,dx&=-\cos x+C\\[8pt]\int\cos x\,dx&=\sin x+C\\[8pt]\int\sec^2x\,dx&=\tan x+C\\[8pt]\int\csc^2x\,dx&=-\cot x+C\\[8pt]\int\sec x\tan x\,dx&=\sec x+C\\[8pt]\int\csc x\cot x\,dx&=-\csc x+C\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\int\tan x\,dx&=-\ln|\cos x|+C\\\int\cot x\,dx&=\ln|\sin x|+C\\\int\sec x\,dx&=\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C\\\int\csc x\,dx&=\ln|\csc x-\cot x|+C\end{aligned}$$ Work on an interval without a pole. For a linear inner expression $ax+b$, divide the antiderivative by $a$.
Inverse-tangent form, for $a>0$: $$\int\frac{1}{a^2+x^2}\,dx=\frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)+C.$$
Inverse-sine form, for $a>0$: $$\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}\,dx=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)+C.$$ Its derivative is finite for $|x|<a$.

examples.title: Rewrite before applying a rule
examples.question: Evaluate $\int\left(6\sqrt{x}+\dfrac{5}{x^2}-\dfrac{2}{x}\right)dx$, $x>0$.
examples.plan: Change every term into a power of $x$. Then the power rule and the $\dfrac1x$ rule apply directly.

steps.why: The power rule works only on the form $x^n$. Roots and fractions must become powers first.
Dividing by $\frac32$ is the same as multiplying by $\frac23$, and $6\cdot\frac23=4$.
The new power is $-1$, so you divide by $-1$.
The power $-1$ needs the logarithm rule. Here $x>0$, so $|x|=x$.

steps.do: Combine the three parts and add one constant $C$.
steps.why: One constant is enough, because the sum of constants is again a constant.

examples.title: Scale an inverse-trigonometric form
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{16+9x^2}\,dx$.
examples.plan: The form $\dfrac{1}{a^2+x^2}$ gives $\tan^{-1}$. First make the coefficient of $x^2$ equal to $1$.

steps.why: The standard form needs $x^2$ alone, with coefficient $1$.
Here $a^2=\dfrac{16}{9}$, so $a=\dfrac43$.
The factor $\dfrac1a$ is $\dfrac34$. Also $x\div\dfrac43=\dfrac{3x}{4}$.
Check: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{3x}{4}=\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+\frac{9x^2}{16}}=\dfrac{12}{16+9x^2}$. Multiply by $\dfrac1{12}$ to get the integrand.

trap: The coefficient in $\int \frac{dx}{a^2+x^2}$ is $\frac{1}{a}$, not $\frac{1}{a^2}$.
answer: $\frac32e^{2x}+\frac15\sin5x+C$.

types.title: Divide by a power of x
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3+5x^2-4}{x^2}\,dx$.
types.plan: The denominator is a single term. Divide each term of the numerator by it.

steps.why: A single-term denominator divides every term separately.
Use the power rule on each term.
Two minus signs make a plus.

types.type: Divide, then use the power rule

types.title: Use a trigonometric rule
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{2-3\sin x}{\cos^2x}\,dx$.
types.plan: Split the fraction. Each part becomes a function from the formula bank.

steps.why: $\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2x}=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}\cdot\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\sec x\tan x$.

steps.do: Use $\int\sec^2x\,dx=\tan x$ and $\int\sec x\tan x\,dx=\sec x$.
steps.why: These are derivative rules read backwards.

types.title: Use an identity to remove a square
types.question: Evaluate $\int\tan^2x\,dx$.
types.plan: There is no direct rule for $\tan^2x$. The identity $\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$ changes it into two known integrals.

steps.why: This comes from $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$.
Each part is in the formula bank.

types.title: Exponential functions
types.question: Evaluate $\int\left(e^{3x}+2^x\right)dx$.
types.plan: For $e^{ax}$ divide by $a$. For $b^x$ divide by $\ln b$.

steps.why: Differentiating $e^{3x}$ gives $3e^{3x}$, so integration divides by $3$.
Differentiating $2^x$ gives $2^x\ln 2$, so integration divides by $\ln2$.

title: Substitution: recognise the inner derivative
lead: A good substitution removes complexity from both the expression and its differential.
ideas: The chain rule says $\frac{d}{dx}F(g(x))=F\prime(g(x))g\prime(x)$. Reverse it: $$\int f(g(x))g\prime(x)\,dx=\int f(u)\,du,\qquad u=g(x).$$ Write $du$ explicitly. If only a constant factor is missing, compensate for that factor outside the integral.

Three useful signals are $\frac{f\prime}{f}$, $f\prime\,f^n$ and $\frac{f\prime}{\sqrt{f}}$. They lead to $\ln|f|$, $\frac{f^{n+1}}{n+1}$ and $2\sqrt f$, respectively. The first formula requires $f\ne0$.
For a definite integral, change the bounds at the same time. You may keep the new variable throughout; there is no need to substitute back before evaluating.

examples.title: A derivative hidden in the numerator
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{4x+3}{2x^2+3x+7}\,dx$.
examples.plan: Differentiate the denominator: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(2x^2+3x+7)=4x+3$. That is exactly the numerator. This is the $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ type.

steps.why: Choose the expression whose derivative appears elsewhere in the integrand.
Now the numerator together with $dx$ becomes $du$.
A complicated integral became the simplest logarithm integral.
The discriminant $9-56<0$ and the leading coefficient is positive. So $2x^2+3x+7>0$, and the modulus is not needed.

examples.title: Change the limits too
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^2 x\sqrt{3x^2+1}\,dx$.
examples.plan: Inside the root is $3x^2+1$. Its derivative is $6x$, and the factor $x$ is outside. Only the constant $6$ is missing.

steps.why: This replaces the factor $x\,dx$ completely.

steps.do: Change the limits: $x=0\Rightarrow u=1$ and $x=2\Rightarrow u=13$.
steps.why: With new limits you never return to $x$.
The root is now a simple power.
The power rule gives $\dfrac{u^{\frac32}}{\frac32}$.
Upper value minus lower value.

trap: After changing to $u$, do not use the old $x$-bounds on an antiderivative in $u$.

types.title: A linear expression inside a power
types.question: Evaluate $\int(3x-2)^5\,dx$.
types.plan: Expanding a fifth power is long. Put $u=3x-2$ instead.

steps.why: The derivative of a linear expression is a constant.
The power rule works on $u^5$.
Shortcut for every linear inside: integrate as usual, then divide by the coefficient of $x$.

types.title: A function times its derivative
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{(\ln x)^2}{x}\,dx$.
types.plan: $\dfrac1x$ is the derivative of $\ln x$. So this is $f(x)^2\cdot f'(x)$.

steps.why: The factor $\dfrac1x\,dx$ is exactly $du$.
A power of $u$ with $du$ is a direct power rule.

types.title: An exponential with an inverse function
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{e^{\tan^{-1}x}}{1+x^2}\,dx$.
types.plan: $\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}$ is the derivative of $\tan^{-1}x$, which sits in the power.

steps.why: The whole fraction with $dx$ becomes $du$.
The exponential is its own antiderivative.

types.title: Derive the rule for tan x
types.question: Show that $\int\tan x\,dx=\ln|\sec x|+C$.
types.plan: Write $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$. The numerator is minus the derivative of the denominator.

steps.why: Then $\sin x\,dx=-du$.
This is the $\dfrac{f'}{f}$ type with a minus sign.

steps.do: Use a log law: $-\ln|\cos x|=\ln\left|\dfrac{1}{\cos x}\right|=\ln|\sec x|$.
steps.why: Both forms are correct. Textbooks often use $\ln|\sec x|$.

title: Rational functions: divide, factor, decompose
lead: The denominator tells you which simpler fractions are possible.
ideas: If the numerator degree is at least the denominator degree, divide first. For distinct linear factors use $\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{x-b}$. A repeated factor $(x-a)^m$ needs every power from $1$ to $m$. An irreducible quadratic needs a linear numerator.

After clearing denominators, compare coefficients or substitute convenient values. For a quadratic denominator, try writing the numerator as a multiple of its derivative plus a constant; complete the square for the leftover part.

examples.title: Repeated factors
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{2x+5}{(x+1)^2(x+3)}\,dx$.
examples.plan: The fraction is proper: degree $1$ is less than degree $3$. The factor $(x+1)$ repeats, so it needs two fractions, one for each power.

steps.why: A repeated factor $(x+1)^2$ needs both $\dfrac{A}{x+1}$ and $\dfrac{B}{(x+1)^2}$.
Multiply both sides by $(x+1)^2(x+3)$.
At $x=-1$ the $A$ term and the $D$ term become zero.
At $x=-3$ the $A$ term and the $B$ term become zero.
The left side has no $x^2$ term. Check with $x=0$: $3A+3B+D=\frac34+\frac92-\frac14=5$.
$\int(x+1)^{-2}\,dx=-(x+1)^{-1}$ by the power rule.

examples.title: A quadratic that does not factor over the reals
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{3x+8}{x^2+4x+8}\,dx$.
examples.plan: The discriminant is $16-32<0$, so the denominator does not factor. Split the numerator into a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, plus a constant.

steps.do: The derivative of the denominator is $2x+4$.
steps.why: This part will give a logarithm.
Choose $\dfrac32$ to match $3x$. Then $\dfrac32\cdot4=6$, and $8-6=2$ remains.
Now each integral has a known type.
It is the $\dfrac{f'}{f}$ type. The quadratic is always positive.
Use $\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{u^2+a^2}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac ua$ with $u=x+2$ and $a=2$.

trap: For $(x+1)^2$, writing only $\frac{A}{(x+1)^2}$ loses a necessary term.
answer: Divide to get $1+\frac{2}{x^2+1}$. The result is $x+2\tan^{-1}x+C$.

types.title: Distinct linear factors
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{x}{(x+1)(x+2)}\,dx$.
types.plan: Two different linear factors give two simple fractions.

steps.why: Multiply both sides by $(x+1)(x+2)$.
Each choice makes one bracket zero.
Each simple fraction gives a logarithm.

types.title: An improper fraction: divide first
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2+1}{x^2-5x+6}\,dx$.
types.plan: Numerator and denominator have the same degree. Divide first, then use partial fractions on the remainder.

steps.why: So the fraction is $1+\dfrac{5x-5}{(x-2)(x-3)}$.
These are the partial fractions $\dfrac{A}{x-2}+\dfrac{B}{x-3}$.
Check with $x=0$: $-3A-2B=15-20=-5$, and $5(0)-5=-5$. The values are correct.
The $1$ integrates to $x$.

types.title: Substitute first, then partial fractions
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{\cos x}{(1-\sin x)(2-\sin x)}\,dx$.
types.plan: Only $\sin x$ appears, and $\cos x\,dx$ is its derivative. Put $t=\sin x$ to get a rational function.

steps.why: Now the integrand is an ordinary rational function.
These are the fractions $\dfrac{A}{1-t}+\dfrac{B}{2-t}$.
The coefficient of $t$ is $-1$, so each logarithm gets a minus sign.
Combine the logarithms with a log law.

title: Integration by parts: make the next integral easier
lead: Choose the factor that becomes simpler when differentiated.
ideas: From $(uv)\prime=u\prime v+uv\prime$, $$\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du.$$ Choose a differentiable $u$ and a $dv$ you can actually integrate. A memory aid about the order of functions is only a starting point; judge the integral that remains.
For powers of $x$ multiplied by an exponential or sine/cosine, repeat parts until the polynomial disappears. Some integrals return to the original integral; collect those terms algebraically.

examples.title: Two rounds of parts
examples.question: Evaluate $\int x^2e^{2x}\,dx$.
examples.plan: A polynomial times an exponential. Differentiate the polynomial, because it becomes simpler each time. Integrate the exponential.

steps.why: It comes from the product rule $(uv)'=u'v+uv'$.
After one differentiation, $x^2$ becomes $2x$, which is simpler.
The new integral has $x$ instead of $x^2$. That is progress.
Now the polynomial disappears completely.
Keep the bracket: minus times minus gives plus for the last term.

examples.title: When the original integral returns
examples.question: Evaluate $I=\int e^x\cos2x\,dx$.
examples.plan: Neither factor becomes simpler. After two rounds of parts the original integral appears again. Then solve for $I$ like an equation.

steps.why: The derivative of $\cos2x$ is $-2\sin2x$. Two minus signs make a plus.
Keep $e^x$ as $dv$ in both rounds. If you switch, the second round undoes the first.
The unknown $I$ appears on both sides.
Add $4I$ to both sides, then divide by $5$.

trap: The minus sign in $uv-\int v\,du$ is essential; a negative derivative can then turn that subtraction into addition.
answer: Parts gives $[\frac{x^2\ln x}{2}-\frac{x^2}{4}]_1^e=\frac{e^2+1}{4}$.

types.title: x times a trigonometric function
types.question: Evaluate $\int x\sin x\,dx$.
types.plan: Differentiate $x$ (it becomes $1$). Integrate $\sin x$.

steps.why: The integral of $\sin x$ is $-\cos x$.
Watch the two minus signs.
Now no product remains.

types.title: A single logarithm
types.question: Evaluate $\int\ln x\,dx$.
types.plan: There is only one function. Write it as $\ln x\cdot1$ and take $dv=dx$.

steps.why: We can differentiate $\ln x$ but we do not yet know its integral.
The $x$ cancels and leaves an easy integral.

types.title: An inverse trigonometric function
types.question: Evaluate $\int\tan^{-1}x\,dx$.
types.plan: Same idea as $\ln x$: take $u=\tan^{-1}x$ and $dv=dx$.

steps.why: The derivative of $\tan^{-1}x$ is a simple fraction.
The new integral is the $\dfrac{f'}{f}$ type, up to a factor $\dfrac12$.
The derivative of $1+x^2$ is $2x$.

types.title: The pattern $e^x\left[f(x)+f'(x)\right]$
types.question: Evaluate $\int e^x\left(\tan x+\sec^2x\right)dx$.
types.plan: Rule: $\int e^x\left[f(x)+f'(x)\right]dx=e^xf(x)+C$. Look for a function and its derivative added together.

steps.why: This is the product rule. Reading it backwards gives the rule.
The bracket is exactly $f+f'$.

title: Trigonometric powers and rationalisation
lead: Use identities to create a substitution, rather than expanding blindly.
ideas: For $\sin^m x\cos^n x$, save a cosine factor if $n$ is odd and use $u=\sin x$; save a sine factor if $m$ is odd and use $u=\cos x$. If both powers are even, half-angle identities reduce them.

For a rational expression in $\sin x$ and $\cos x$, $t=\tan (\frac{x}{2})$ gives $\sin x=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$, $\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$ and $dx=\frac{2dt}{1+t^2}$. It is a general method, but a simpler substitution should be preferred when available.
In a definite integral, split the interval if the chosen tangent substitution has a pole inside it. Algebraic cancellation must not hide a discontinuity.

examples.title: Odd cosine power
examples.question: Evaluate $\int\sin^4x\cos^3x\,dx$.
examples.plan: Cosine has an odd power. Keep one $\cos x$ to make $d(\sin x)$. Change the remaining $\cos^2x$ into sine.

steps.why: Use $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$.
Everything except $\cos x$ is now in terms of $\sin x$.
A trigonometric integral became a polynomial.
Then put $u=\sin x$ back.

examples.title: A half-angle substitution
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{dx}{2+\sin x}$.
examples.plan: No simpler pattern works. The substitution $t=\tan\dfrac x2$ turns any rational function of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ into a rational function of $t$.

steps.why: These come from the double-angle formulas and $dt=\dfrac12\sec^2\dfrac x2\,dx$.
Change the limits together with the variable.
Use a common denominator $1+t^2$.
The factors $1+t^2$ and $2$ cancel.
Now the $\tan^{-1}$ form applies.
At $t=1$: $\tan^{-1}\sqrt3=\dfrac\pi3$. At $t=0$: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac1{\sqrt3}=\dfrac\pi6$.

trap: An identity such as $\sqrt{\cos^2x}=\cos x$ is false when $\cos x<0$; the root is $|\cos x|$.
answer: Use $\frac{1-\cos 4x}{2}$: $\frac{x}{2}-\frac{\sin 4x}{8}+C$.

types.title: Square of a sine
types.question: Evaluate $\int\sin^2(2x+5)\,dx$.
types.plan: An even power has no spare factor. Use $\sin^2\theta=\dfrac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}$ to lower the power.

steps.why: Here $\theta=2x+5$, so $2\theta=4x+10$.
For $\cos(4x+10)$, divide by the coefficient $4$.

types.title: Product of two different angles
types.question: Evaluate $\int\sin3x\cos4x\,dx$.
types.plan: Change the product into a sum: $2\sin A\cos B=\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)$.

steps.why: $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$.
$\int\sin7x\,dx=-\dfrac{\cos7x}{7}$ and $\int\sin x\,dx=-\cos x$.

types.title: Odd power of sine alone
types.question: Evaluate $\int\sin^3x\,dx$.
types.plan: Odd power: keep one $\sin x$ for $d(\cos x)$. Change $\sin^2x$ into $1-\cos^2x$.

steps.why: Use $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$.
The minus sign comes from $du=-\sin x\,dx$.

title: Radicals and standard algebraic forms
lead: Choose a substitution that turns the root into a familiar identity.
ideas: For $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$, use $x=a\sin\theta$ with a range where $\cos\theta\ge0$. For $\sqrt{x^2+a^2}$, use $x=a\tan\theta$. For $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$, a secant substitution works on a suitable interval.

Useful results, for $a>0$, are $$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}=\ln|x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}|+C,$$ $$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}=\ln|x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}|+C,$$ and $$\int\frac{dx}{x^2-a^2}=\frac1{2a}\ln\left|\frac{x-a}{x+a}\right|+C.$$ Respect the real domain and avoid the poles.
Completing the square connects a general quadratic radical to these forms. For a numerator $px+q$, separate a multiple of the derivative of the quadratic before making a more elaborate substitution.

examples.title: Derive the semicircle antiderivative
examples.question: Evaluate $\int\sqrt{9-x^2}\,dx$, $|x|<3$.
examples.plan: A root of $a^2-x^2$ with $a=3$. Put $x=3\sin\theta$, because $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$ removes the root.

steps.why: On this range $\cos\theta>0$, so the root has no sign problem.
Use $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$.
Remember to replace $dx$ as well as the root.
Use $\cos^2\theta=\dfrac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}$.
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{9-x^2}}{3}$ from a right triangle with hypotenuse $3$ and opposite side $x$.
This is the general formula $\int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx=\frac x2\sqrt{a^2-x^2}+\frac{a^2}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac xa+C$ with $a=3$.

examples.title: A root made linear
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}+3}$, $x>0$.
examples.plan: The root causes the difficulty. Give it a name, $t=\sqrt x$. Then the integrand becomes a rational function of $t$.

steps.why: Change $dx$ too, not only the root.
The degree on top equals the degree below, so divide.
Because $2t=2(t+3)-6$.
Then put $t=\sqrt x$ back. Since $\sqrt x+3>0$, the modulus is not needed.

trap: Carry the transformed $dx$ through the substitution; replacing just the radical is not enough.
answer: With $u=x+2$, the answer is $\sin^{-1} (\frac{x+2}{4})+C$, for $|x+2|<4$.

types.title: The form $\dfrac{1}{x^2-a^2}$
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2-16}$.
types.plan: $x^2-16=(x-4)(x+4)$. Use $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2-a^2}=\frac1{2a}\ln\left|\frac{x-a}{x+a}\right|+C$ with $a=4$.

steps.why: This shows where the formula comes from.
Each fraction gives a logarithm.

types.title: Complete the square under a root
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+2x+2}}$.
types.plan: Complete the square to reach the form $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u^2+a^2}}$.

steps.why: Half of $2$ is $1$, and $2-1=1$.
Use $\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{u^2+a^2}}=\ln\left|u+\sqrt{u^2+a^2}\right|+C$ with $a=1$.

types.title: A linear numerator over a root
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{x^2+2x+3}}\,dx$.
types.plan: Write the numerator as (a multiple of the derivative of the quadratic) + (a constant). The first part gives a root, the second gives a logarithm.

steps.why: Choose $\dfrac12$ to match $x$. Then $1$ is left over.
This is the $\dfrac{f'}{\sqrt f}$ type, which gives $2\sqrt f$.
Complete the square: $x^2+2x+3=(x+1)^2+2$.

types.title: The root of a quadratic
types.question: Evaluate $\int\sqrt{x^2+4x+6}\,dx$.
types.plan: Complete the square, then use $\int\sqrt{u^2+a^2}\,du=\frac u2\sqrt{u^2+a^2}+\frac{a^2}{2}\ln\left|u+\sqrt{u^2+a^2}\right|+C$.

steps.why: Half of $4$ is $2$, and $6-4=2$.

title: Definite integrals: accumulation and the fundamental theorem
lead: The area picture explains both the signs and the endpoint subtraction.
ideas: For continuous $f$, let $A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dt$. A small increase $h$ adds a thin strip with approximate signed area $f(x)h$. Taking the limit gives $A\prime(x)=f(x)$.
If $F\prime=f$, then $A-F$ has derivative zero; evaluate at $a$ to obtain $$\int_a^b f(x)dx=F(b)-F(a).$$ Also $\int_a^b f=-\int_b^a f$ and $\int_a^b f+\int_b^c f=\int_a^c f$.
Geometric area uses $\int_a^b|f(x)|dx$. Signed accumulation uses $\int_a^b f(x)dx$. These agree only when the integrand is nonnegative throughout the interval.

examples.title: A zero integral can hide nonzero area
examples.question: Compare $\displaystyle\int_0^2(x-1)\,dx$ with $\displaystyle\int_0^2|x-1|\,dx$.
examples.plan: The line $y=x-1$ is below the $x$-axis for $x<1$ and above it for $x>1$. Signed area and true area are different.

steps.why: The triangle below the axis cancels the triangle above it.

steps.do: Remove the modulus: $|x-1|=1-x$ on $[0,1]$ and $|x-1|=x-1$ on $[1,2]$.
steps.why: Split the interval where the expression inside changes sign.
This is the area of the left triangle.
This is the area of the right triangle.
Zero accumulated change does not mean that nothing happened.

examples.title: Do not integrate through a pole
examples.question: Why is $\left[-\dfrac{1}{x}\right]_{-1}^1=-2$ not the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1 \frac{dx}{x^2}$?
examples.plan: Before you use $F(b)-F(a)$, check that the integrand is continuous on the whole interval. Here $\dfrac1{x^2}$ is not defined at $x=0$.

steps.why: But $\dfrac1{x^2}>0$, so a negative answer is impossible. Something is wrong.

steps.do: Find the problem: $x=0$ is inside $[-1,1]$, and $\dfrac1{x^2}\to\infty$ there.
steps.why: The fundamental theorem needs a continuous integrand.

steps.do: Look at the right part: $\displaystyle\int_\varepsilon^1 x^{-2}\,dx=\frac1\varepsilon-1\to\infty$ as $\varepsilon\to0^+$.
steps.why: The area near zero has no finite value. The left part is the same by symmetry.

examples.result: The integral does not exist (it diverges). The formula $F(b)-F(a)$ was used across a discontinuity.

trap: Continuity is a sufficient hypothesis for the form of the fundamental theorem used here. Check it before using the formula mechanically.
answer: $A(2)=0$ because its bounds coincide; $A\prime(2)=2^2+1=5$.

types.title: Direct use of the fundamental theorem
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^2\left(4x^3-5x^2+6x+9\right)dx$.
types.plan: Find one antiderivative, then subtract its value at the lower limit from its value at the upper limit. No $+C$ is needed.

steps.why: Integrate each term with the power rule.
Substitute the upper limit.
Substitute the lower limit.
Any constant $C$ cancels in the subtraction.

types.title: A trigonometric definite integral
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\cos^2x\,dx$.
types.plan: Lower the power with $\cos^2x=\dfrac{1+\cos2x}{2}$, then use the limits.

steps.why: Divide by $2$ for $\cos2x$.
$\sin\pi=0$ and $\sin0=0$.

types.title: A standard form with limits
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_2^3\frac{dx}{x^2-1}$.
types.plan: Use $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2-a^2}=\frac1{2a}\ln\left|\frac{x-a}{x+a}\right|$ with $a=1$.

steps.why: The interval $[2,3]$ avoids the poles $x=\pm1$.
Use $\ln a-\ln b=\ln\dfrac ab$.

types.title: Substitution in a definite integral
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 xe^{x^2}\,dx$.
types.plan: $x$ is half the derivative of $x^2$. Put $u=x^2$ and change the limits.

steps.why: So $x\,dx=\dfrac{du}{2}$.

title: Reflection: make two difficult integrands add to something simple
lead: Before searching for an antiderivative, compare the integrand with its mirror image.
ideas: The substitution $x=a+b-t$ proves $$\int_a^b f(x)dx=\int_a^b f(a+b-x)dx.$$ The reversed limits and negative differential cancel. If the sum of the two integrands simplifies, add the two expressions for the same integral.

On $[0,a]$, if $f(a-x)=f(x)$, then $$\int_0^a xf(x)dx=\frac a2\int_0^a f(x)dx.$$ Proof: reflection changes $x$ to $a-x$ while leaving $f$ unchanged; add the two forms. More generally, split any weight into a symmetric part and an antisymmetric part about $\frac{a}{2}$.
A common pattern is $\frac{h(x)}{h(x)+h(a-x)}$ with a nonzero denominator: its integral is $\frac{a}{2}$. For sine and cosine on $[0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$, reflection interchanges the two functions.

examples.title: A high power that does not need expansion
examples.question: Evaluate $I=\displaystyle\int_0^4 \frac{(x+2)^5}{(x+2)^5+(6-x)^5}\,dx$.
examples.plan: Property: $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x)\,dx=\int_0^a f(a-x)\,dx$. Here $a=4$. Replacing $x$ by $4-x$ swaps $x+2$ and $6-x$.

steps.why: So the numerator changes, but the denominator only changes order.
This is the same number $I$, written in a different way.
The two numerators add to the denominator.
On $[0,4]$ both $x+2$ and $6-x$ are positive, so the denominator is never zero.

examples.title: A symmetric weight
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^3 x\left[\left(x-\frac{3}{2}\right)^4+2\right]dx$.
examples.plan: Call the bracket $f(x)$. It does not change when $x$ becomes $3-x$. Then the factor $x$ can be replaced by its average value $\dfrac32$.

steps.why: An even power removes the sign.
Replace $x$ by $3-x$ everywhere.
The integrand is even, so double the right half.
$\left(\dfrac32\right)^5=\dfrac{243}{32}$, and dividing by $5$ gives $\dfrac{243}{160}$.
Multiply the fractions.

trap: The weighted midpoint identity needs symmetry of $f$; it is not true for every integrand.
answer: Reflection interchanges numerator terms, giving twice the integral as $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Answer: $\frac{\pi}{4}$.

types.title: The classic square-root pair
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\frac{\sqrt{\sin x}}{\sqrt{\sin x}+\sqrt{\cos x}}\,dx$.
types.plan: On $\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]$, replacing $x$ by $\dfrac\pi2-x$ changes $\sin$ into $\cos$ and $\cos$ into $\sin$.

steps.do: By the property, $I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\frac{\sqrt{\cos x}}{\sqrt{\cos x}+\sqrt{\sin x}}\,dx$.
steps.why: $\sin\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)=\cos x$ and $\cos\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)=\sin x$.
The numerators add to the denominator.

types.title: Remove the x by reflection
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}\,dx$.
types.plan: $\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x$. So replacing $x$ by $\pi-x$ changes only the factor $x$.

steps.why: The awkward factor $x$ disappears.

steps.do: The new integrand is symmetric about $\dfrac\pi2$: $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}=2\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}$.
steps.why: For $\int_0^{2a}$: if $f(2a-x)=f(x)$, the integral is twice $\int_0^a$.
Use $1+\cos x=2\cos^2\dfrac x2$.
$\tan\dfrac\pi4=1$.
Put the pieces back together.

title: Parity, periodicity and weighted periods
lead: Translate the interval when the symmetry is not centred at zero.
ideas: If $f(-x)=-f(x)$, an integrable odd function has zero integral over $[-a,a]$. If $f(-x)=f(x)$, the integral is twice its value over $[0,a]$. A shift $u=x-c$ reveals symmetry about $x=c$.
For an integrable function of period $T$, every interval of length $T$ has the same integral, and $\int_0^{nT}f=n\int_0^T f$. Split the interval into complete periods and a remainder.

For a weighted periodic integral, let $A=\int_0^T f(t)dt$ and $B=\int_0^T tf(t)dt$. In the $k$th period use $x=t+kT$. Summing gives $$\int_0^{nT}xf(x)dx=nB+\frac{Tn(n-1)}2A.$$ The weight itself is not periodic.

examples.title: Oddness hidden by a shift
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^5 \frac{(x-3)^3}{1+(x-3)^2}\,dx$.
examples.plan: The centre of $[1,5]$ is $3$. Shift the variable so that the centre becomes $0$. Then test whether the integrand is odd or even.

steps.why: Now the interval is symmetric about zero.
Same integral, new name for the variable.
An odd function has $g(-u)=-g(u)$.

steps.do: An odd continuous function on $[-a,a]$ has integral $0$.
steps.why: The area on the left exactly cancels the area on the right.

examples.title: Weighted repeating arches
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{3\pi}x|\sin x|\,dx$.
examples.plan: $|\sin x|$ repeats every $\pi$ (three equal arches). The factor $x$ grows, so treat each arch separately.

steps.why: Each piece covers one arch.

steps.do: In arch $k$ put $x=t+k\pi$ with $t\in[0,\pi]$. Then $|\sin x|=\sin t$.
steps.why: Shifting by a multiple of $\pi$ does not change $|\sin x|$.

steps.do: Arch $k$ gives $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi(t+k\pi)\sin t\,dt=\int_0^\pi t\sin t\,dt+k\pi\int_0^\pi\sin t\,dt$.
steps.why: Split the bracket.

steps.do: $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi t\sin t\,dt=\left[-t\cos t+\sin t\right]_0^\pi=\pi$ and $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\sin t\,dt=2$.
steps.why: The first one uses integration by parts.

trap: An odd function with a nonintegrable singularity does not automatically have an integral of zero.
answer: The period is $\pi$ and one-period integral is $2$. Thus the answer is $8$.

types.title: An odd power over a symmetric interval
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-\frac\pi2}^{\frac\pi2}\sin^7x\,dx$.
types.plan: Test for odd or even before you integrate anything.

steps.do: $\sin^7(-x)=(-\sin x)^7=-\sin^7x$. So the integrand is odd.
steps.why: An odd power keeps the minus sign.

steps.do: The interval is symmetric about $0$, so the integral is $0$.
steps.why: No calculation is needed.

types.title: Separate odd and even parts
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-\frac\pi2}^{\frac\pi2}\left(x^3+x\cos x+\tan^5x+1\right)dx$.
types.plan: Test each term separately. Odd terms give $0$. Only the even terms need work.

steps.why: For example, $(-x)\cos(-x)=-x\cos x$.
The constant $1$ is even. Its integral is the length of the interval.

types.title: An even function
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\left(x^4+|x|\right)dx$.
types.plan: An even function has $f(-x)=f(x)$. Its integral on $[-a,a]$ is twice the integral on $[0,a]$.

steps.why: Both terms are even.
On $[0,1]$, $|x|=x$, so the modulus disappears.

types.title: The property for $[0,\,2a]$
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\cos^5x\,dx$.
types.plan: Property: if $f(2a-x)=-f(x)$, then $\displaystyle\int_0^{2a}f(x)\,dx=0$. Here $2a=\pi$.

steps.why: $\cos(\pi-x)=-\cos x$.

steps.do: The second half cancels the first half, so the integral is $0$.
steps.why: The graph on $\left[\dfrac\pi2,\pi\right]$ is the first half turned upside down.

title: Modulus, floor and fractional part
lead: Split exactly where the formula changes.
ideas: For $|g(x)|$, locate all zeros of $g$ in the interval, make a sign chart, and integrate the correct signed expression on each subinterval. For $\lfloor g(x)\rfloor$, split where $g(x)$ crosses an integer.
The fractional part is $\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$. On $[k,k+1)$, use $x=k+t$ so that $\{x\}=t$. A value at an isolated endpoint does not change a Riemann integral.
Do not replace $\lfloor x^2\rfloor$ by $(\lfloor x\rfloor)^2$. The breakpoints of the former occur at square roots of integers.

examples.title: A floor function inside a product
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^2x\lfloor x^2\rfloor\,dx$.
examples.plan: $\lfloor x^2\rfloor$ changes only when $x^2$ crosses a whole number. Put $u=x^2$ so that the jumps sit at $u=1,2,3$.

steps.why: The factor $x$ is exactly what this substitution needs.
Now the floor function has its jumps at whole numbers.
Each piece has width $1$, so its area equals its height.
Multiply by $\dfrac12$.

examples.title: A weighted fractional part
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^3x\{x\}\,dx$.
examples.plan: $\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$. On each unit interval $[k,k+1)$, write $x=k+t$ so that $\{x\}=t$.

steps.why: The fractional part is the distance from the last whole number.
Integrate in $t$ from $0$ to $1$.
Put each value of $k$.
Common denominator $6$.

trap: For a nonmonotone inner function, the same integer may be crossed more than once. Find every breakpoint.

types.title: One modulus
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-5}^{5}|x+2|\,dx$.
types.plan: $x+2$ changes sign at $x=-2$. Split there.

steps.why: Test a point in each part.
Each is a triangle: $\dfrac12\cdot3\cdot3$ and $\dfrac12\cdot7\cdot7$.
Both parts are areas, so they add.

types.title: A sum of moduli
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^4\left(|x-1|+|x-2|+|x-3|\right)dx$.
types.plan: Integrate each modulus separately. Each one is a pair of triangles.

steps.why: $x-1\ge0$ on $[1,4]$: one triangle with base $3$ and height $3$.
Split at $2$: triangles with sides $1$ and $2$.
Split at $3$: triangles with sides $2$ and $1$.
Add the three results.

types.title: A modulus of a cubic
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2}\left|x^3-x\right|dx$.
types.plan: $x^3-x=x(x-1)(x+1)$ has zeros at $-1$, $0$ and $1$. Make a sign chart and split at each zero inside the interval.

steps.do: Signs: positive on $(-1,0)$, negative on $(0,1)$, positive on $(1,2)$.
steps.why: Test $x=-\frac12$, $x=\frac12$ and $x=\frac32$.
$F(-1)=\dfrac14-\dfrac12=-\dfrac14$.
The minus sign makes the negative part positive.
Add all the pieces.

title: Riemann sums: read the width and the sample point
lead: A sum becomes an integral only after its scaling is identified.
ideas: For continuous $f$ on $[a,b]$, $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{b-a}{n}\sum_{r=1}^n f\left(a+\frac{(b-a)r}{n}\right)=\int_a^b f(x)dx.$$ Left endpoints and midpoint samples have the same limit. The factor $\frac{b-a}{n}$ is the strip width.
In rational sums, divide each occurrence of $r$ by $n$ and factor out the matching power of $n$. Check that one overall factor $\frac{1}{n}$ remains. Missing this factor changes the limit completely.

Finite products can be handled by logarithms when all factors are positive. A product of many factors close to $1$ often becomes an exponential of an integral; justify the approximation uniformly over the samples.

examples.title: A disguised sum
examples.question: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{r=1}^n \frac{n}{4n^2+r^2}$.
examples.plan: A Riemann sum on $[0,1]$ looks like $\dfrac1n\displaystyle\sum f\left(\frac rn\right)$. Make $\dfrac1n$ and $\dfrac rn$ appear.

steps.do: Divide top and bottom by $n^2$: $\dfrac{n}{4n^2+r^2}=\dfrac1n\cdot\dfrac{1}{4+\left(\frac rn\right)^2}$.
steps.why: Now every $r$ appears as $\dfrac rn$.

steps.do: So the sum is $\dfrac1n\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^n f\left(\frac rn\right)$ with $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{4+x^2}$.
steps.why: The strip width is $\dfrac1n$ and the sample points are $\dfrac rn$.
$\dfrac rn$ runs from nearly $0$ to $1$.
Use the $\tan^{-1}$ form with $a=2$.

examples.title: A product becomes accumulation
examples.question: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\prod_{r=1}^n\left(1+\frac{2r}{n^2}\right)$.
examples.plan: A product of many factors: take the logarithm. A logarithm changes a product into a sum.

steps.why: $\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b$.
For small $u$, $\ln(1+u)$ is very close to $u$.
Use $1+2+\dots+n=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$.
So the error disappears in the limit.
Undo the logarithm.

trap: Not every expression containing a sum is a Riemann sum. Establish both the sample points and their width.
answer: The limit is $\int_0^1\sqrt{1+3x}dx=\frac{14}{9}$.

title: Variable limits, integral equations and local behaviour
lead: Differentiate the accumulated quantity before trying to evaluate it.
ideas: For continuous $f$ and differentiable bounds, $$\frac d{dx}\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}f(t)dt=f(v(x))v\prime(x)-f(u(x))u\prime(x).$$ Both endpoint chain-rule factors matter.

An equation defining $f$ through an integral may turn into a differential equation. After differentiating, retain the value obtained from the original equation at a convenient point; differentiation alone can lose that condition.
For $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dt$, zeros of $f$ are stationary points of $F$. They are extrema only when $f$ changes sign. The sign chart is often more useful than an explicit formula for $F$.

examples.title: Both endpoints move
examples.question: Find $F'(1)$ if $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_x^{x^2+1}\frac{dt}{1+t^2}$.
examples.plan: Leibniz rule: value at the upper limit times its derivative, minus value at the lower limit times its derivative.

steps.why: Find both limits and their derivatives first.
Put each limit into the integrand $\dfrac1{1+t^2}$.

examples.title: An integral equation
examples.question: Continuous $f$ satisfies $f(x)=3+\displaystyle\int_0^x2t f(t)\,dt$. Find $f(1)$.
examples.plan: Differentiate both sides to remove the integral. Keep the starting value from $x=0$.

steps.why: An integral from $0$ to $0$ is zero.
The derivative of $\displaystyle\int_0^x g(t)\,dt$ is $g(x)$.
So $e^{-x^2}f(x)$ is a constant.
Use $x=0$ to find it.

examples.title: A stationary point without a turn
examples.question: For $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x(t-1)^2(t-3)\,dt$, classify the stationary points.
examples.plan: $F'(x)$ is the integrand at $x$. Use a sign chart of $F'$, not a formula for $F$.

steps.why: These are the stationary points.
$(x-1)^2\ge0$ always, so the sign comes from $x-3$.

steps.do: At $x=1$ the sign does not change: not a maximum or minimum.
steps.why: $F$ keeps decreasing through $x=1$.

steps.do: At $x=3$ the sign changes from $-$ to $+$: local minimum.
steps.why: $F$ stops decreasing and starts increasing.

trap: The integration variable is a dummy variable; differentiate through the moving bounds, not by treating that dummy variable as $x$.
answer: Write $H=x\int_0^x(t^2+2)dt-\int_0^xt(t^2+2)dt$. Endpoint terms cancel in $H\prime$, so $H\prime\prime=x^2+2$ and the answer is $3$.

title: Inverse functions and composition
lead: A difficult inverse can disappear after changing the variable.
ideas: Let $g$ be continuously differentiable and strictly monotone on $[a,b]$. Substitution $y=g(x)$ and integration by parts give $$\int_{g(a)}^{g(b)}g^{-1}(y)dy=[xg(x)]_a^b-\int_a^b g(x)dx.$$ The oriented-limit form also works for a decreasing $g$.
For an integral of $f(g(x))g\prime(x)$, substitute $u=g(x)$ directly. The same idea works when $f$ is defined implicitly, or when $f$ itself is an accumulated integral.

examples.title: No cubic inverse formula needed
examples.question: $g(x)=x^3+2x$ on $[1,2]$. Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_3^{12}g^{-1}(y)\,dy$.
examples.plan: Do not try to find $g^{-1}$. Put $y=g(x)$, then integrate by parts.

steps.why: An increasing function has an inverse. The limits $3$ and $12$ come from $x=1$ and $x=2$.
The inverse function disappears.
Take $u=x$ and $dv=g'(x)\,dx$.
Ordinary power rule.
Subtract.

examples.title: A nested accumulated function
examples.question: Let $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x e^{-t^2}\,dt$ and $F(2)=c$. Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^2 F(x)e^{-x^2}\,dx$.
examples.plan: $e^{-x^2}$ is the derivative of $F(x)$. So this is the $f\cdot f'$ type.

steps.why: Differentiating an integral with upper limit $x$ gives the integrand.
The new limits come from $F$.
We never need a formula for $F$.

trap: An inverse-function formula needs a one-to-one function on the selected interval; a globally nonmonotone function may still work on a suitable restricted interval.
answer: The boundary term is $3(8)-0(2)=24$. Subtract $14$ to obtain $10$.

title: Reduction formulae and beta-type integrals
lead: Relate the difficult integral to a simpler member of the same family.
ideas: Let $I_n=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin^n xdx$. Integration by parts with $u=\sin^{n-1}x$ and $dv=\sin xdx$ gives $I_n=(n-1)(I_{n-2}-I_n)$ for integer $n\ge2$. Therefore $$I_n=\frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2},\qquad I_0=\frac{\pi}{2},\ I_1=1.$$

For nonnegative integers $m,n$, repeated parts gives $$\int_0^1x^m(1-x)^ndx=\frac{m!n!}{(m+n+1)!}.$$ To see the recurrence, integrate $(1-x)^n$ and differentiate $x^m$: $B_{m,n}=\frac{mB_{m-1,n+1}}{n+1}$ for $m\ge1$. Finish with $B_{0,k}=\frac{1}{k+1}$.
Reflection also gives $B_{m,n}=B_{n,m}$. This is a useful independent check and a quick way to choose the shorter reduction.

examples.title: A high even power
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin^8 x\,dx$.
examples.plan: Use the reduction formula $I_n=\dfrac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}$ again and again until you reach $I_0=\dfrac\pi2$.

steps.why: Each step lowers the power by $2$.
Multiply all the fractions.
Divide top and bottom by $3$.

examples.title: An exact rational value
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1x^3(1-x)^2\,dx$.
examples.plan: Use $\displaystyle\int_0^1x^m(1-x)^n\,dx=\frac{m!\,n!}{(m+n+1)!}$ with $m=3$, $n=2$. Then check by expanding.

steps.why: Expanding is short for small powers.
Both methods agree.

trap: Do not use the integer factorial formula for arbitrary real exponents without replacing factorials by the appropriate beta/gamma expressions and checking convergence.
answer: The integral is $\frac{1!4!}{6!}=\frac{1}{30}$, so the required value is $1$.

title: Inequalities and least possible values
lead: Sometimes a bound is the answer; an antiderivative is unnecessary.
ideas: If $m\le f\le M$ on $[a,b]$ with $a<b$, then $m(b-a)\le\int_a^bf\le M(b-a)$. Pointwise inequalities integrate in the same direction. If a continuous nonnegative function is positive somewhere, its integral is strictly positive.

Integrate a square: $\int(f-cg)^2\ge0$ for every real $c$. The discriminant of this quadratic in $c$ cannot be positive. This proves Cauchy–Schwarz: $$(\int_a^b fg)^2\le(\int_a^bf^2)(\int_a^bg^2).$$ Equality holds when the two functions are proportional (apart from sets of integral measure zero).
With $g=1$, $\int_a^b f^2\ge\frac{(\int_a^bf)^2}{b-a}$. Always test whether the equality function is allowed by every condition.

examples.title: A lower bound with an attainable equality
examples.question: Continuous $f$ on $[0,2]$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_0^2f=8$. Find the least possible $\displaystyle\int_0^2f^2$.
examples.plan: A square is never negative. Compare $f$ with its average value $\dfrac82=4$.

steps.why: The integral of a non-negative function is non-negative.
Use $\int f=8$ and $\int_0^216\,dx=32$.
This is a lower bound.
A function reaches the bound, so $32$ is the least value.

examples.title: Two constraints require a better comparison
examples.question: Continuous $f$ on $[0,1]$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_0^1f=0$ and $\displaystyle\int_0^1xf=2$. Find the least $\displaystyle\int_0^1f^2$.
examples.plan: Combine the two conditions into one, then use the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $\left(\int gh\right)^2\le\int g^2\int h^2$.

steps.why: Subtracting $\dfrac12\int f=0$ changes nothing.
Square both sides of the first result.
$\left[\dfrac{\left(x-\frac12\right)^3}{3}\right]_0^1=\dfrac{1}{24}+\dfrac1{24}$.
$\int_0^1x\left(x-\frac12\right)dx=\frac13-\frac14=\frac1{12}$.

steps.do: $f=24x-12$ satisfies both conditions and gives $\displaystyle\int f^2=576\cdot\frac1{12}=48$.
steps.why: So the bound is reached.

trap: A numerical lower bound is not necessarily a minimum: you must show an admissible function attains equality.
check: For positive continuous $f$ on $[0,1]$ with $\int f=3$, prove $\int \frac{1}{f}\ge\frac{1}{3}$.
answer: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to $\sqrt f$ and $\frac{1}{\sqrt f}$: $1\le(\int f)(\int\frac{1}{f})=3\int\frac{1}{f}$. Equality holds for $f=3$.

title: Parameters inside integrals
lead: A parameter can turn an awkward logarithm into a rational function.
ideas: If $f(x,a)$ and its partial derivative with respect to $a$ are continuous on a fixed compact rectangle, then $$\frac d{da}\int_u^v f(x,a)dx=\int_u^v\frac{\partial f}{\partial a}(x,a)dx.$$ This is a sufficient condition; improper endpoint cases require additional justification.
Use an easy parameter value to determine the integration constant after integrating back. A parameter method is not complete until that value is checked.
If endpoints also depend on the parameter, include their contributions as well as the integral of the partial derivative.

examples.title: A logarithmic integral
examples.question: For $a>0$, evaluate $I(a)=\displaystyle\int_0^1\ln(1+ax)\,dx$.
examples.plan: A single logarithm: integrate by parts with $dv=dx$.

steps.why: $u=\ln(1+ax)$, $du=\dfrac{a}{1+ax}dx$, $v=x$.
Add and subtract $1$ in the numerator.
Divide by $a$ for the linear inside.
Common denominator $a$. As $a\to0$ this tends to $0$, which matches $\int_0^1\ln1\,dx=0$.

examples.title: A moving parameter and a moving endpoint
examples.question: Find $H'(a)$ for $H(a)=\displaystyle\int_0^a\ln(1+at)\,dt$, $a>0$.
examples.plan: The parameter $a$ is in the upper limit and inside the integrand. Both give a term.

steps.why: Endpoint term plus the derivative under the integral.
Here $t$ is treated as a constant.
Collect the logarithms.

trap: If you differentiate only the integrand when the bounds move, the endpoint terms are lost.
answer: Continuity permits differentiation under the integral. At $a=0$ the integrand is $x$, so the answer is $\frac{1}{2}$.

title: Logarithmic symmetry and improper endpoints
lead: A singular endpoint may still have a finite integral, but it must be handled as a limit.
ideas: Near zero, $\ln x$ diverges, yet $\int_0^1\ln xdx=-1$ because $x\ln x\to0$. By contrast, $\int_0^1\frac{dx}{x}$ diverges. A large value near an endpoint alone does not decide convergence.

To derive the log-sine result, put $L=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\ln (\sin x)dx$. Reflection gives the same value with cosine. Therefore $2L=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\ln (\sin 2x)dx-(\frac{\pi}{2})\ln 2$. Substituting $u=2x$ and reflecting on $[0,\pi]$ makes the first integral equal to $L$. Thus $$L=-\frac\pi2\ln2.$$ The logarithmic endpoint singularities are integrable, so these changes can be justified by truncated limits.
For a parameter $a>0$, $\ln(a\sin x)=\ln a+\ln(\sin x)$. This simple separation produces many exact values without inventing a new antiderivative.

examples.title: A shifted log-sine value
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\ln (4\sin x)\,dx$.
examples.plan: Split the logarithm. Then use the known value $L=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\ln\sin x\,dx=-\frac\pi2\ln2$.

steps.why: $\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b$.
Add the value of $L$.

examples.title: An improper integral with a symmetric weight
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi x\ln(2\sin x)\,dx$.
examples.plan: $\ln(2\sin x)$ is unchanged by $x\to\pi-x$. So the factor $x$ can be replaced by its average $\dfrac\pi2$.

steps.why: $\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x$. The singularities at $0$ and $\pi$ are integrable.
Same method as in Session 9.
$\int_0^\pi\ln\sin x\,dx=2L$ by symmetry about $\dfrac\pi2$.

trap: Do not apply a remembered log-sine or symmetry result to a different angle without checking the interval and transformed function.
answer: Split as $\ln\sin x-\ln\cos x$. The two convergent improper integrals agree by reflection, giving $0$.

title: Combine two ideas: a demanding problem is often two familiar steps
lead: Look for what can be simplified before committing to a long calculation.
ideas: A useful sequence is: check the domain; look for a symmetry; simplify the transformed sum; then choose a substitution or inequality. Several advanced questions become short only after the first structural observation.
When $f(x)+f(a-x)$ is known, you may determine an integral against a symmetric weight without determining $f$. If the weight is not symmetric, separate it into its reflected sum and difference first.

examples.title: A functional relation with a weight
examples.question: Continuous $f$ satisfies $f(x)+f(2-x)=x^2-2x+8$ on $[0,2]$. Find $I=\displaystyle\int_0^2(x-1)^2f(x)\,dx$.
examples.plan: We do not know $f$, but we know $f(x)+f(2-x)$. Reflection creates exactly that sum.

steps.why: The unknown function disappears.
Even integrand: double $\int_0^1$.
Divide by $2$.

examples.title: Reflection followed by tangent substitution
examples.question: Evaluate $I=\displaystyle\int_0^\pi \frac{x\sin^2 x}{3+\cos^2 x}\,dx$.
examples.plan: The fraction is unchanged by $x\to\pi-x$. So $I=\dfrac\pi2J$, with $J$ the integral without $x$.

steps.why: Reflect and add, as in Session 9.
Make the numerator look like the denominator.
The integrand is symmetric about $\dfrac\pi2$.
Put the pieces together.

examples.title: Minimise an integral with respect to a constant
examples.question: Find the minimum of $J(a)=\displaystyle\int_0^3(x^2-a)^2\,dx$ over real $a$.
examples.plan: After integration, $J(a)$ is a quadratic in $a$. Complete the square.

steps.why: $a$ is a constant during integration.
Complete the square.
A square is smallest when it is zero.

trap: A long expression does not necessarily need a long antiderivative. First ask which part stays unchanged by reflection or substitution.
answer: The weight is symmetric. Twice the required integral is $6\int_{-2}^2u^2du=32$. The answer is $16$.

title: Limits involving accumulated functions
lead: Use the local behaviour of the integrand and keep the first nonzero term.
ideas: If $f$ is continuous at $a$, the average over a shrinking interval tends to $f(a)$: $\lim_{h\to0}\frac1h\int_a^{a+h}f(t)dt=f(a)$. This works from either side with oriented limits.

When the leading term vanishes, expand to the necessary order, or apply the fundamental theorem and L’Hôpital’s rule where its hypotheses hold. An expansion $f(t)=c t^m+o(t^m)$ near zero gives $\int_0^xf(t)dt=\frac{cx^{m+1}}{m+1}+o(x^{m+1})$ for integer $m\ge0$.

For two moving bounds near the same point, account for the difference of the corresponding powers. Do not replace a small integral by its width times a value that is itself zero without examining the next term.

examples.title: A vanishing first-order term
examples.question: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1}{x^3}\int_0^x\ln(1+2t^2)\,dt$.
examples.plan: Both top and bottom tend to $0$. Use L'Hôpital's rule with the fundamental theorem.

steps.why: An integral from $0$ to $0$ is $0$.
The derivative of $\int_0^xg(t)\,dt$ is $g(x)$.
Here $u=2x^2\to0$.

examples.title: Two endpoints, one small interval
examples.question: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1}{x^3}\int_x^{2x}(1-\cos t)\,dt$.
examples.plan: Form $\dfrac00$. Differentiate with the Leibniz rule.

steps.why: Upper limit $2x$ gives the factor $2$.
$1-\cos2x\approx\dfrac{4x^2}{2}=2x^2$.
The $x^2$ cancels.

trap: If the denominator vanishes to third order, a first-order approximation may be too weak to determine the limit.
answer: $\sin3t=3t+O(t^3)$ gives an integral $\frac{3x^2}{2}+O(x^4)$, hence $\frac{3}{2}$.

title: Recurrences, bounds and a limiting constant
lead: Two relations can determine an asymptotic value without an explicit formula.
ideas: Let $R_n=\int_0^1\frac{x^n}{1+x}dx$. The identity $\frac{x^n}{1+x}+\frac{x^{n+1}}{1+x}=x^n$ gives $R_n+R_{n+1}=\frac{1}{n+1}$. Since $0<x<1$, the sequence is positive and decreasing.

To find its scale, write $\frac{1}{1+x}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1-x}{2(1+x)}$. Then $$0\le R_n-\frac1{2(n+1)}\le\frac12\int_0^1x^n(1-x)dx=\frac1{2(n+1)(n+2)}.$$ Multiplication by $n+1$ and squeezing gives $(n+1)R_n\to\frac{1}{2}$.
This method explains why samples close to $x=1$ dominate: $x^n$ becomes small away from that endpoint. The coefficient is the endpoint value of the remaining continuous factor.

examples.title: Use a recurrence to avoid long division
examples.question: Find $R_3=\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x^3}{1+x}\,dx$.
examples.plan: Let $R_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x^n}{1+x}dx$. Adding two neighbours gives $R_n+R_{n+1}=\displaystyle\int_0^1x^n\,dx=\frac1{n+1}$.

steps.why: Start of the chain.
Use the relation with $n=0$.
Use the relation with $n=1$.
Use the relation with $n=2$.

examples.title: A different endpoint coefficient
examples.question: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}(n+1)\int_0^1\frac{x^n}{2+x}\,dx$.
examples.plan: For large $n$, $x^n$ is tiny except near $x=1$. So $\dfrac1{2+x}$ acts like $\dfrac13$. Make this exact with a bound.

steps.why: $\int_0^1x^n\,dx=\dfrac1{n+1}$.
On $[0,1]$, $\dfrac1{2+x}\le\dfrac12$.

steps.do: Multiply by $n+1$: the error is at most $\dfrac{1}{6(n+2)}\to0$.
steps.why: So only the main part remains.

trap: From $R_n+R_{n+1}\to0$ alone you cannot infer the value of $nR_n$; scaling needs a quantitative bound.
answer: The expression is $3+\frac{n+1}{n+2}$, so the limit is $4$.

title: Reciprocal substitutions on an infinite interval
lead: The transformation $x\mapsto\frac{1}{x}$ can exchange powers in the numerator.
ideas: In a convergent improper integral on $(0,\infty)$, $x=\frac{1}{t}$ changes $dx$ to $-\frac{dt}{t^2}$. Track both the differential and reversed limits. This can pair rational functions of $x$ and $\frac{1}{x}$.
An improper substitution can be justified on finite truncated intervals and then by taking limits. Establish convergence before combining the transformed expressions.

examples.title: Pair two rational integrals
examples.question: Evaluate $I=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty \frac{dx}{x^4+5x^2+1}$.
examples.plan: The substitution $x=\dfrac1t$ gives a partner integral. Adding the two creates the pattern $\left(1+\dfrac1{x^2}\right)dx=d\left(x-\dfrac1x\right)$.

steps.do: The integral converges: near $0$ it is bounded, and near $\infty$ it behaves like $\dfrac1{x^4}$.
steps.why: Always check that an infinite integral exists.
The limits swap, and the minus sign swaps them back.
Divide top and bottom by $x^2$.
As $x$ goes from $0$ to $\infty$, $u$ goes from $-\infty$ to $\infty$.
$\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{du}{u^2+a^2}=\frac\pi a$.

examples.title: A family, with its condition
examples.question: For $a>-2$, evaluate $I(a)=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty \frac{dx}{x^4+ax^2+1}$.
examples.plan: Repeat the same method with $a$ in place of $5$.

steps.why: So the denominator is never zero when $a>-2$.
Same steps as the example above.
At $a=-2$ the denominator is zero at $x=1$, and the integral does not exist.

trap: The parameter condition is part of the result. An expression containing a square root is not proof that the original integral converges.
answer: Reciprocal substitution makes this equal to $I(7)$. The result is $\frac{\pi}{6}$.
